flawed_step: lines 0014-0016 ('Moreover, f cannot belong to T1 ...')
counterexample: V = {x, y}, T1 = T2 = {{x,y}}. Then e = {x,y}, VA = {x}, VB = {y}, the unique T2-path from x to y is the single edge e, so j = 1 and f = {v0, v1} = {x,y} = e. Hence f DOES belong to T1, contradicting the proof's claim; the parenthetical argument silently assumes f != e, which is exactly what fails here. (The theorem itself still holds in this case: T1' = T1 and T2' = T2.)
reasoning_summary: 0001 'Solution' header - no content to verify. 0002 e = {x,y} arbitrary edge of T1 chosen; legitimate universal-instantiation start, and x != y since e is an edge of a (simple) tree. 0002-0003 'removing e disconnects T1 into exactly two components, each a tree' - correct standard fact: every edge of a tree is a bridge, and each component of T1\{e} is acyclic and connected. 0003-0004 naming the components A, B with vertex sets VA, VB and x in VA, y in VB - justified, since x and y lie in different components after deleting the bridge e. 0004-0005 'VA, VB partition V and e is the unique T1-edge joining VA to VB' - justified: T1 spans V so the two components cover V disjointly, and any second crossing edge would keep T1\{e} connected across the cut, contradicting the previous step. 0006 'T2 connected, so there is a unique path in T2 from x to y' - correct: in a tree any two vertices are joined by exactly one path. 0007-0009 writing the path as x = v0 - v1 - ... - vk = y with each consecutive pair an edge of T2 - just notation for the path, valid. 0009-0011 'there is 1 <= j <= k with v_{j-1} in VA and v_j in VB' - justified: v0 in VA, vk in VB, and {VA,VB} partitions V, so take the least index with v_j in VB. 0012 definition f := {v_{j-1}, v_j} - well defined by the previous step. 0013-0014 'f is an edge of T2 and has one endpoint in VA, the other in VB' - justified: consecutive path vertices form a T2-edge, and by the choice of j the endpoints straddle the cut. 0014-0016 'Moreover, f cannot belong to T1 (otherwise T1 would contain an edge connecting VA and VB other than e)' - FAILS: the parenthetical tacitly assumes f != e, which is unjustified and actually false whenever e is also an edge of T2 (then the unique T2-path from x to y is the single edge e, forcing f = e in T1). The correct claim provable here is only f not in T1\{e}. The assertion as stated is false, so this step is not justified. 0017-0028 defining E'_1 = (T1\{e}) u {f}, E'_2 = (T2\{f}) u {e}, T1' , T2' and stating the claim - definitions only, valid. 0029-0033 '|E'_1| = |T1| = |V|-1, since one edge was removed and one added' - the conclusion is true (f not in T1\{e}, and if f = e then E'_1 = T1), but as written it leans on the erroneous step 0014-0016; the count itself is correct. 0033-0038 'T1\{e} is two disjoint trees A, B, and f joins v_{j-1} in VA to v_j in VB, so T1' is connected on V' - justified: A and B are each connected and span VA, VB, and f bridges the cut. 0039-0043 'T1' is acyclic: there was no A u B path between v_{j-1} and v_j, so adding f creates no cycle' - justified, since the two endpoints lie in distinct components of T1\{e}; adding an edge between different components never creates a cycle. 0043-0046 'connected, |V|-1 edges, no cycles, hence a spanning tree of V' - correct (connected + acyclic on vertex set V already suffices). 0047-0050 '|E'_2| = |T2| = |V|-1' - the value is correct (e in T2 forces f = e, so e is not in T2\{f}), though the proof does not explicitly verify e not in T2\{f}; a minor omission, not a false statement. 0050-0051 'removing f disconnects T2 into two components' - correct, every tree edge is a bridge. 0051-0052 'since f lies on the unique x-y path of T2, deleting f separates x from y' - justified: any x-y path in T2\{f} would be a second distinct x-y path in T2. 0053-0056 'adding e = {x,y} reconnects the two components, so T2' is connected and spans V' - justified, e joins the two sides. 0056-0058 'no cycle is created by e, since T2\{f} has no x-y path (else T2 would have two distinct x-y paths)' - justified, same uniqueness argument. 0058-0060 'T2' is connected, acyclic, |V|-1 edges, hence a tree' - correct. 0061-0065 conclusion restating the existence claim for arbitrary e in T1 - the overall theorem does follow from the surviving steps. 0066 page number, no content. Overall: the construction and both tree verifications are sound and the theorem is genuinely established, but the explicit assertion at lines 0014-0016 that f cannot belong to T1 is false in the degenerate case e in T1 n T2, so that step fails the step-by-step justification requirement.
